title: BlueHarbor Post-Incident Hardening & Handoff
summary: Follow-up bridgecall after a multi-region latency surge that caused degraded throughput for BlueHarbor's shipping APIs. Reviewed root cause hypotheses, immediate mitigations applied, longer-term hardening plan, and ownership for runbook and rollback steps. Agreed on KV cache validation, traffic shaping policy, and a small staged rollout for the failover model; Redwood to deliver artifacts and a verification checklist before the pilot. Customer raised SOC2 and data residency questions for Private deployment plan.
topics: Incident root cause review (KV cache + batching bump)
Longer-term mitigations: validation, autoscaling policy, traffic shaping
action_items: Jon Richter - produce KV cache validation patch and rollout plan - due 2026-05-22
Maya Patel - share pricing delta and dedicated pool sizing options - due 2026-05-18
Li Chen - schedule dry-run pilot with BlueHarbor staging environment - due 2026-05-20
Ravi Sinha (Customer) - provide redacted telemetry slice and access window for testing - due 2026-05-19
next_steps: Redwood to send hardened runbook + fallback flow (by 2026-05-18)
Pilot dry-run in BlueHarbor staging (target week of 2026-05-25)
Security/Compliance deep-dive with risk & SOC2 docs (schedule week of 2026-05-18)
Follow-up sync after dry-run to confirm metrics and go/no-go (2026-05-29)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-16 16:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel, Jon Richter, Li Chen (Redwood) / Aisha Khan, Tom Reeves, Erin Cole, Ravi Sinha, Olga Petrova (BlueHarbor)

Summary (auto): quick sync after last night's degradation; triage notes, mitigation validation, runbook handoff, compliance questions.

[00:00] Maya: okay everyone, thanks for hopping on. we wanted to keep this tight — 60 minutes — and make sure we leave with clear owners. is that still good on your side?
[00:12] Aisha: yes, thanks Maya. we got woken up last night, so appreciate the follow-up. want to understand the root cause and how we avoid this next month when volume spikes.
[00:20] Jon: quick recap from our side, i'll try to be succinct. we saw a concurrent increase in long-tail token generation from two flows which amplified KV cache evictions. that led to higher per-request compute and some backpressure in the batching layer. batching then increased latency which pushed more requests into longer windows — bad feedback loop.
[00:40] Tom: yeah, that's what we saw on our end, latency stayed high for about 18 minutes even after we flipped the emergency throttle. some requests timed out at the app tier.
[00:53] Jon: exact numbers were in the log slice you shared — the hot prefix frequency went from 0.8% to 6.4% during the spike, which is what stressed the prefix cache heuristics.
[01:10] Erin: when you say prefix cache heuristics — can you explain quickly for product folks? like, what did the heuristic do wrong?
[01:22] Jon: sure. so the runtime keeps a KV cache for recent key-values for serving long chats efficiently. heuristics decide which prefixes to evict when memory pressure grows. during the surge the heuristic underestimated the value of certain mid-length keys and evicted them, causing regen of KV and re-computation. it's subtle — not a correctness bug, more of a policy tuning issue.
[01:45] Olga: i'm hearing both cache and batching contributed. we also had some spike in small-batch requests which reduced batching efficiency.
[02:00] Li: thanks, Olga, that's consistent. quick note: the emergency throttle did reduce incoming qps by about 30% within 3 minutes and that helped, but the degraded tail lingered.
[02:15] Maya: action-wise, we already pushed a temporary mitigation yesterday evening that adjusted the eviction threshold and forced sticky caching for the top prefixes for your workload. jon, can you say if that was sufficient?
[02:31] Jon: the temporary patch brought tail latency back to baseline in staging within 10 minutes — in prod it came back too but took roughly 12-14 minutes. we did not see error rates spike after the patch.
[02:45] Ravi: quick interrupt — from security, i need to know if that sticky caching change keeps any extra customer data in memory longer than before. any PI/PHI concerns?
[02:58] Jon: no PI wasn't added; it's still ephemeral model state. we only changed eviction timing for prefix keys, not persistent storage. but we'll add a note to the runbook about retention assumptions.
[03:14] Aisha: thanks. i'd also like to hear about root cause validation — how confident are you that the heuristic is the primary factor vs some external burst pattern from our side (we did release a marketing campaign last week)?
[03:30] Jon: good point. we correlated your traffic with the hot prefixes; there was overlap. so it's likely both: your traffic pattern amplified the heuristic flaw. we should treat this as a combined workload-heuristic failure mode.
[03:45] Tom: what's the definitive remediation then — a code fix, revised heuristic, or operational guardrails?
[03:52] Jon: short term: validation patch to make eviction decisions conservative for hot prefixes (deployed). medium: telemetry-driven adaptive thresholding so the runtime responds to burst patterns. long term: workload-aware pre-warming and a KV cache integrity check that runs during scale events.
[04:12] Erin: pre-warming — that sounds like pre-loading expected prefixes. do we need to ship a manifest?
[04:20] Jon: ideally yes. we can accept a small manifest or let the runtime learn from a training window. for now, we recommended a small static list for your top 500 prefixes.
[04:34] Maya: okay, change of topic: can we talk about failover and rollback? last night your team rolled to emergency throttle and then a manual downgrade to a smaller model family. how did that affect your SLA calculations?
[04:50] Tom: the downgrade saved CPU but increased percent of degraded outputs for a small subset. customers noticed, so we had complaints. SLA-wise, we want a fallback that preserves correctness more than throughput.
[05:05] Jon: we can configure a graceful degrade flow: first try smaller model with a different cost/latency profile, if signal quality falls below threshold, route to an isolation pool using the default model but limit qps. it's a policy we'll add to the runbook.
[05:22] Aisha: that sounds sensible. also, we're evaluating a private deployment for compliance reasons — any risks there if we move to managed private?
[05:31] Maya: important question. Redwood Private gives you a customer VPC control plane and KMS integration, but we'll need to walk through SOC2 docs, encryption at rest keys (HSM or KMS), and audit log retention. li, can you own scheduling the compliance deep-dive?
[05:45] Li: yep, i'll get that scheduled. we'll share SOC2 scope, architecture diagrams, and a template for audit logs.
[05:54] Ravi: our security asks for proof of deterministic data residency and key separation — can you show separation between control plane and model telemetry?
[06:04] Jon: yes, for Private we can separate telemetry pipelines and optionally relay telemetry via your collector. we'll enumerate the flows in the security whitepaper.
[06:15] Olga: concerning the pilot timeline — when can we run a dry-run in staging? we need at least two maintenance windows.
[06:23] Maya: we proposed week of 2026-05-25 for a dry-run. li will coordinate windows and redwood will provide the runbook checklist.
[06:35] Erin: what success metrics should we hold the pilot to? latency p50/p95/p99, error rate, and cost delta?
[06:44] Jon: yes, baseline p50/p95/p99, end-to-end error rate, user-facing correctness (we can metricize from your evaluation set), and cost per 1k tokens. also measure KV cache miss rate.
[06:58] Tom: can you log KV miss rate at 1s granularity during the dry-run? we need fine-grained telemetry.
[07:06] Jon: yes, we can add that. expect a lightweight telemetry hook; we'll coordinate retention windows with your telemetry team.
[07:18] Aisha: on ownership, who will be our point-of-contact for the runbook changes and the pilot?
[07:24] Maya: redwood POC is Jon for technical + Li for coordination. i'll be the commercial owner.
[07:31] Maya: okay let's talk about the runbook contents quickly — what will be in there?
[07:36] Jon: doc will include incident signals, mitigation steps (emergency throttle, model fallback), rollback steps, validation checks (KV cache checksums, prefix hit ratios), and communication templates.
[07:48] Ravi: add a security checklist for any runtime changes and a note about KMS key rotation.
[07:54] Jon: will do. we'll include a KMS checklist and flag when a change touches key material.
[08:01] Erin: what about traffic shaping policy — you mentioned autoscaling earlier. can we throttle gracefully by route?
[08:08] Jon: yes, routing policy per path is supported. we can set soft quotas with graceful degradation and hard limits. we'll recommend route-level soft quotas tied to SLOs.
[08:20] Olga: any blockers on implementing the KV integrity check in runtime? time estimate?
[08:26] Jon: low risk for a lightweight integrity check (checksum + sample replay) — 3 sprints to fully automate, but we can ship a manual validation script in a week.
[08:38] Aisha: good. we'd prefer the manual script first so we can validate in staging.
[08:44] Jon: understood. i'll supply the script and docs.
[08:49] Maya: moving to compliance, li can you outline items we'll send?
[08:53] Li: we'll share SOC2 attestation, architecture diagram for Private, audit log retention policy, data flow diagram, and a guide to KMS integration.
[09:03] Ravi: also want a list of subcontractors and where logs live.
[09:07] Li: yep, that'll be in the security package.
[09:10] Tom: one ask — can Redwood produce a short postmortem we can share internally? high level timeline + mitigations + next steps.
[09:19] Maya: absolutely. we'll produce a customer-friendly postmortem and a technical RCA.
[09:24] Aisha: timeframe?
[09:26] Maya: we'll aim for the public-friendly postmortem by 2026-05-18 and the deep technical RCA by 2026-05-22.
[09:34] Erin: any risks with the suggested staged rollout?
[09:36] Jon: main risk is underestimating tail patterns; we'll reduce blast radius with canary percentages and time-based ramping.
[09:44] Olga: and do we have automated rollback triggers?
[09:47] Jon: yes, we can set automated rollback based on p99 and error rate thresholds. we'll include threshold values in the runbook but want to tune them with you during dry-run.
[09:58] Aisha: okay let's capture final owners and dates.
[10:02] Maya: read back? jon for technical artifacts and script; li for scheduling and security package; maya for pricing and commercial; ravi for customer telemetry slice.
[10:12] Tom: agreed.
[10:15] Maya: any outstanding questions?
[10:18] Ravi: one last from security — are logs retained outside your control for hosted? need clarity on retention and purging.
[10:26] Li: for hosted we retain telemetry for 90 days by default; for private we can align to your retention policy. we'll document purge procedures.
[10:36] Aisha: good. thanks everyone. let's reconvene after the dry-run.
[10:42] Maya: thanks all — we'll follow up with the runbook and schedule.

Recap (auto):
- Temporary patch applied last night stabilized tail latency but longer term fixes required.
- Action items assigned: KV cache patch, runbook, security package, pilot scheduling.
- Pilot dry-run scheduled target week of 2026-05-25; follow-up sync set for 2026-05-29.
